lines.trans: Look at what they hand out right at our door!
What is this strange bright paper?
Nearby a new restaurant is opening today.
They call themselves the best restaurant in town.
They brazenly hand out advertisements to our guests!
Could they really be promising tastier food?
They write that with them it is much better.
Chef, you should not be so nervous.
I will go and chase away this insolent fellow.
We simply must show top quality.
Our restaurant is the best in all Moscow!
Not a single regular guest of ours will leave.
Let them try opening properly first!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'more'.

examples.trans: We need a more objective assessment.

examples.text: Погоди, нам нужна более объективная оценка.
examples.trans: Wait, we need a more objective opinion.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'paper', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('paper, official document') (colloquial) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Here is a document from the prosecutor's office.

examples.text: Вот бумага из прокуратуры. Слушание будет сегодня вечером.
examples.trans: Here is an order from the prosecutor's office. The hearing will be this evening.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('tasty, delicious').

examples.trans: The bread rings are very tasty.

examples.text: Марина Сергеевна, присядьте. Попробуйте чай с сушками, очень вкусные.
examples.trans: Marina Sergeyevna, have a seat. Try the tea with bread rings, they're very tasty.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'high', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Common masculine noun meaning 'town, city' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Abstract masculine noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-ость', denoting the quality or state of 'guest'.

examples.trans: All the guests love them very much.

examples.text: Сегодня вечером к нам придут гости.
examples.trans: Guests are coming to our place tonight.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'door' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The door is behind the wardrobe.
Open the door. Is this flat nine?

meanings.note: + infinitive; agrees with the subject: должна (f)
Secondary conversational sense ('owe') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Жадность, Паша, должна быть умеренная. Комнатной температуры.
examples.trans: Greed, Pasha, should be moderate. Room temperature.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'food', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: В этом ресторане всегда свежая еда.
examples.trans: There is always fresh food in this restaurant.
Oh no, bad food? Does your stomach hurt?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('behind') (+ instrumental) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'class', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('classroom') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('cool!, great!') (colloquial exclamation) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Вот это настоящий высший класс кулинарного искусства!
examples.trans: Now that is true top class in culinary art!

meanings.note: лучший в мире = the best in the world
Secondary conversational sense ('better') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ты мне даёшь пятьсот рублей, а я выхожу и покупаю тебе лучшую приставку в мире.
examples.trans: You give me five hundred roubles, and I get out and buy you the best console in the world.

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'impudently'.

examples.text: Он нагло врал прямо в глаза.
examples.trans: He brazenly lied straight to the face.
Why are you lying so boldly?

examples.text: Ты просто нагло и открыто сейчас блефуешь!
examples.trans: You are simply insolently and openly bluffing now!

meanings.note: showing a lack of respect in a rude or aggressive manner

examples.trans: That was a very insolent act.
Be quiet right now, insolent rump!

meanings.en: must, need to, it is necessary
meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'it is necessary'.

examples.trans: We need to do even more.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'зывать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to call', forming an aspectual pair with 'назвать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to designate') (to assign a title) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Call me simply Lev from now on.

examples.text: А вы называйте меня просто Вика.
examples.trans: And you call me simply Vika.

examples.text: Они называют себя лучшим рестораном города.
examples.trans: They call themselves the best restaurant in town.

meanings.en: much, far, a lot (before a comparative)
meanings.note: намного хуже = much worse; намного лучше = much better

examples.trans: In prison it will be much worse.

examples.text: Но я же вижу, как тебе плохо. В тюрьме будет намного хуже, поверь мне.
examples.trans: But I can see how bad things are for you. In prison it will be much worse, believe me.

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates

Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'рвничать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to be nervous', forming an aspectual pair with 'разнервничаться'.

examples.trans: Don't be nervous, everything is fine.

examples.text: Павел Юрьевич, вам нельзя нервничать сейчас.
examples.trans: Pavel Yuryevich, you mustn't get worked up right now.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('really?') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Неужели так трудно найти хороший сюжет?
examples.trans: Is it really so difficult to find a good story?

examples.text: Неужели президент накажет вас за правду?
examples.trans: Will the president really punish you for the truth?
Do you really not care at all?

meanings.note: + genitive: ни копейки = not a penny
Secondary conversational sense ('...  = neither... nor') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Пятьсот. А у меня ни копейки.
examples.trans: Five hundred. And I haven't got a penny.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('new').

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
examples.trans: Well, happy now? Now I have to look for a new job.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'fine'.
+ dative of the person: обещать вам

examples.text: Марина, я вам обещаю: со стеной ничего не случится.
examples.trans: Marina, I promise you: nothing will happen to the wall.

meanings.note: agrees in gender and case with the noun
Secondary conversational sense ('alone') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('they') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'крываться'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to open'. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.trans: Big cards are opening up for us.

examples.text: У нас сейчас открываются большие карты.
examples.trans: Big cards are opening up for us now.

examples.text: Через неделю они открываются рядом с нами.
examples.trans: In a week they are opening right next to us.

открыться.gloss: to open, to come to light

meanings.en: to come to light, to be revealed
meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'крыться'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to open', forming an aspectual pair with 'открываться'. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.
Secondary conversational sense ('to open') (intransitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: New circumstances have come to light.

examples.text: Прошу внимания. Открылись новые обстоятельства по другому делу.
examples.trans: May I have your attention. New circumstances have come to light in another case.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'boyfriend', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('guy, lad, young man') (informal) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to write', forming an aspectual pair with 'написать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to take notes') (in a lesson) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to go', forming an aspectual pair with 'идти'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to show', paired with 'показывать'.

examples.trans: Shall we show this to Anikeev?

examples.text: Ну, покажите руки. Что у вас за спиной?
examples.trans: Well, show me your hands. What is behind your back?

meanings.en: to try, to taste (food or drink)
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'пробовать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to try', forming an aspectual pair with 'пробовать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to try, to attempt') (+ infinitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Try the tea with bread rings.

meanings.en: to have a look, to take a look
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'смотреть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to have a look', forming an aspectual pair with 'смотреть'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to watch (a film) through') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: постоянный клиент = regular customer
Secondary conversational sense ('permanent, constant') (постоянная работа = permanent job) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The test drive is only for regular clients.

examples.text: Я тоже могу быть постоянным клиентом!
examples.trans: I can be a regular client too!

examples.text: Тест-драйв у нас только для постоянных клиентов.
examples.trans: Our test drive is only for regular clients.

meanings.en: to drive away, chase out, dismiss
meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'гнать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to chase away, drive out'.

examples.trans: Why did you chase him away?

examples.text: Зачем ты его прогнал? Это ошибка.
examples.trans: Why did you chase him away? That is a mistake.
And what if she chases me away?

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'just'.
Secondary conversational sense ('easy') (это просто = it's easy) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'straight'.
Secondary conversational sense ('straight ahead') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: В смысле, Виктор Степанович? Прямо так, да?
examples.trans: What do you mean, Viktor Stepanovich? Just like that?

meanings.note: + 3rd person verb: 'пусть строят' = let them build

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.en: to hand out, to give away, to distribute
meanings.note: Prefix 'раз-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'давать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to hand out, to distribute', paired with 'раздать'.

examples.trans: Were you handing out flats through connections?

examples.text: Вы квартиры очередников по блату раздавали? Я пятнадцать лет в очереди стою!
examples.trans: Did you hand out waiting-list flats through connections? I've been standing in the queue for fifteen years!

examples.text: Вы квартиры очередников по блату раздавали?
examples.trans: Did you hand out waiting-list flats through connections?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'advertisement, advertising' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Они нагло раздают рекламу у ресторана.
examples.trans: They brazenly hand out advertisements near the restaurant.

examples.text: Они нагло раздают рекламу нашим гостям!
examples.trans: They brazenly hand out advertisements to our guests!

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'next to'.
Secondary conversational sense ('nearby, close by') (adverb of place) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: A plot next to Grigory Soprykin.
Right nearby, round the corner, there's a cheburek café.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: А с Пашей я снова чувствую себя женщиной.
examples.trans: And with Pasha I feel like a woman again.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.text: Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
examples.trans: Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'strongly'.

examples.trans: The wind is blowing hard outside.

examples.text: Я так два года потеряла. Любила так сильно!
examples.trans: I lost two years like that. I loved him so much!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'начала').
Secondary conversational sense ('from the beginning, over again') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: First they were rude and insulting over there.
Let's start everything from the beginning.

examples.text: Мы танцевали. Сначала они там грубили, оскорбляли.
examples.trans: We were dancing. First they were rude and insulting over there.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'транный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('strange, odd').
Conversational Russian particle ('so') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('like that, so') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('I have') (possession) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('from (ask from someone)') (просить у кого) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: уже четыре года = for four years now

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.

уйти.gloss: to leave, to go away (on foot)

meanings.en: to leave, to go away, to walk out
meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to leave, to go away (on foot)', paired with 'уходить'.
Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('good, nice').

examples.text: Какое хорошее утро! Лидия Алексеевна, чашку кофе, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: What a lovely morning! Lidia Alekseyevna, a cup of coffee, please.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'bright', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('vivid') (intense in flavor or color) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я просто хотел добавить яркий аромат.
examples.trans: I simply wanted to add a vivid aroma.

examples.text: Что это за странная яркая бумага?
examples.trans: What is this strange bright paper?

examples.text: Дмитрий, почему здесь выключили яркий свет?
examples.trans: Dmitry, why did they turn off the bright light here?
